strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine label noise in preference datasets with clear empirical evidence (20-40% corruption rates)
Elegant theoretical framework connecting arbitrary preference losses to probabilistic models via Gibbs distribution, enabling generalization across multiple algorithms (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 algorithms, 2 models, multiple datasets (UltraFeedback, MultiPref), and benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard)
Consistent empirical improvements (3-7% win rate gains) across all tested configurations, not cherry-picked results
Solid theoretical contribution with Theorem 4.1 providing convergence guarantees and verification through controlled synthetic noise experiments
Practical implementation with clear Algorithm 1, runtime overhead analysis (11% average slowdown), and reproducibility resources provided
Thorough ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis demonstrating robustness
Qualitative analysis showing RE-PO identifies genuinely noisy/reversed preference labels in real datasets
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.1 assumes perfectly calibrated model and full-batch EM, but implementation uses mini-batch gradient updates with EMA (Generalized EM). Theoretical guarantees don't cover the actual algorithm used.

Limited novelty of core technique: EM for noisy labels (Dawid-Skene 1979, Crowd-BT 2013) is well-established. Main contribution is applying existing methods to preference learning, which is somewhat incremental.
No human evaluation despite alignment work targeting human preferences. Automatic LLM-based evaluators (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard) can be biased and don't directly measure alignment quality.

Experimental limitations: Main results treat UltraFeedback as single virtual annotator (K=1), limiting leverage of multi-annotator EM. MultiPref improvements (3-4% LC) substantially weaker than UltraFeedback (4-7% LC).
Hyperparameter sensitivity: Performance highly sensitive to EMA parameter α (30.1% at α=0.001 vs 35.5% at α=0.1). No principled guidance for setting η₀ and α on new datasets.

Synthetic noise experiments (Section 5.5) use uniform noise on small calibrated model, but real preference noise is typically systematic (annotator bias, instruction ambiguity). Gap between verification conditions and real-world applicability.

Theory requires 'perfectly calibrated model' assumption. While paper starts from instruction-tuned LLMs, it acknowledges failure mode if base model is misaligned—this is a significant practical limitation not thoroughly validated.
Limited model scope: Experiments only on 7-8B scale. Generalization to larger/smaller models unclear. Unclear how method performs on model families beyond Mistral/Llama.
Incomplete baseline comparisons: No direct empirical comparison with Selective DPO (mentioned but not evaluated). Mixed results vs. rDPO/Hölder-DPO on some configurations.
Missing analysis of noise characterization: No systematic study of which noise types RE-PO handles best/worst. Limited error analysis or investigation of when confidence scores fail.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine label noise (20-40%) in preference alignment datasets with clear practical impact
Principled EM-based approach with mathematical rigor; Theorem 4.1 provides convergence guarantees for annotator reliability recovery
Elegant Gibbs construction (Eq. 2) generalizing framework across diverse preference losses (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO)
Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple algorithms, models (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B), datasets (UltraFeedback, MultiPref), and benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard)
Consistent improvements across configurations (up to 7.0% on AlpacaEval 2 LC) demonstrating generality
Strong reproducibility: detailed algorithms, proofs, controlled synthetic noise verification (Figure 2), qualitative analysis of identified noisy labels
Practical implementation with measured overhead (~11% average) and hyperparameter ablations
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.1 assumes perfect calibration and full-batch updates; practical implementation uses mini-batch Generalized EM (Eq. 7). Idealized assumptions don't extend to realistic setting, limiting theoretical justification
Limited algorithmic novelty: Core EM approach for unreliable annotators well-established (Dawid-Skene 1979); contribution is primarily application to LLM alignment rather than new techniques

Mixed empirical results with high variance by configuration: SimPO degrades on Llama WR (37.1→39.4 only), label smoothing achieves comparable performance (SimPO: 48.1 vs RE-SimPO: 46.9), no statistical significance testing

Surprisingly strong label smoothing baselines make it unclear whether EM-based approach is fundamentally better; insufficient analysis of relationship between methods and computational overhead justification (11-40%)

Limited exploration of failure modes and method applicability: no systematic analysis of when RE-PO underperforms, when to apply vs. simpler alternatives, or how to select hyperparameters (η₀, α) with unknown noise

Main experiments lack realistic noise: UltraFeedback treated as single virtual annotator; MultiPref multi-annotator evaluation limited to one dataset; synthetic noise may not reflect real annotation patterns
Missing ablations on induced probability formulation (Eq. 2) and analysis of learned vs. ground-truth annotator reliabilities; unclear how method generalizes to extreme noise rates
Presentation issues: claim of 'lifting to general framework' potentially oversold (more meta-wrapper than fundamental framework); dense exposition; insufficient intuitive explanations
